title: "Performance and memory"

## Measure the quantity you mean {#sec-performance-definitions}

| Quantity | Definition and exclusions |
|---|---|
| Warm MHD throughput | `N^3 * iterations / elapsed / 1e6` MCell/s; synchronized timed MHD loop only |
| Phase-average seconds | Sum of a named synchronized production phase divided by measured cycles |
| Production phase total | Sum of the reported phases; not all process wall time |
| End-to-end wall time | Wrapper child-process interval, including startup and output work in that interval |
| Simulation progress | Redshift/physical time reached per wall time under the exact chosen model and tolerances |

A fast bare MHD kernel is not the speed of full chemistry, radiation, gravity,
spectral diagnostics, or checkpointing. A large timestep can improve progress
while changing the trajectory. Report accuracy controls with performance.

## Reproducible kernel benchmark {#sec-kernel-benchmark}

```sh
julia --project=. -t auto scripts/benchmark.jl --backend=cpu --n=32 \
  --iterations=10 --output=docs/data/benchmark-cpu.toml
julia --project=environments/metal -t auto scripts/benchmark.jl \
  --backend=metal --n=32 --iterations=10 --output=docs/data/benchmark-metal.toml
julia --project=environments/cuda -t auto scripts/benchmark.jl \
  --backend=cuda --n=32 --iterations=10 --output=docs/data/benchmark-cuda.toml
```

Run only the relevant backend after bootstrap. The benchmark warms the operator,
resets its initial field before timing, and synchronizes at completion. CPU
uses the reference integrator and GPU uses the cube path; this is not identical
machine instruction work. Record integrator, grid, iterations, Julia threads,
hardware, version, source hash, and scope with the throughput.
{{< src "scripts/benchmark.jl" "Warm compilation" >}}

### Comparing GLM and CT throughput {#sec-kernel-benchmark-ct}

`--mhd-solver=glm|ct|both` selects the solver (default `glm`, unchanged). CT
always runs the `:ref` integrator, so `both` prints one table with GLM on its
default integrator, GLM on `:ref` (the like-for-like integrator for CT), and CT, with the centred
`divB dx/Brms` of every row and the exact face divergence for CT. A case that fails to compile or run is
reported `NOT_RUN` with the reason, not omitted. Outputs default to `results/benchmark*.toml`,
one file per row (`...-glm.toml`, `...-ct.toml`), and carry `mhd_solver`; none
overwrites `docs/data/benchmark-*.toml`.

```sh
julia --project=environments/metal -t 4 scripts/benchmark.jl --backend=metal \
  --n=96 --iterations=60 --mhd-solver=both --output=results/bench-metal-compare.toml
```

Apple M5 Max, N=96, 60 iterations, warm, Float32 (two repeats, 2026-10-24;
the GPU is shared, so repeat before quoting): GLM cube 112.1 and 111.1, CT ref
131.9 and 134.3 MCell/s. CT is the :ref integrator and carries 21 extra arrays per
cell, so this is a kernel-only number, not a production-step speed; the CT step is
also not GLM-limited (its `dt` is the plain CFL step, see
[Comparing CT and GLM runs](validation.qmd#sec-ct-vs-glm)).

GLM `:ref` runs on Metal through the tuple-packed kernel. Same machine, N=96, 60
iterations, Float32, 2026-10-24 (two `--mhd-solver=both` repeats, shared GPU): GLM
cube 101.9 and 100.1, GLM ref 150.5 and 160.8, CT ref 113.2 and 135.3 MCell/s.
In this kernel-only benchmark the cube is therefore not the fastest GLM kernel on
this GPU; the production default is unchanged until a coupled-step comparison says
otherwise.

For physical trajectories the production runner must not advance uncounted
warmup states at a frozen cosmological time. Keep `MHD_WARMUP=0`; use
`MHD_PROFILE_SKIP_CYCLES` to omit startup cycles from timing while preserving
the evolved physical history.

## Production profiles {#sec-production-profiles}

`performance.tsv` and the log separate CFL, bare MHD, radiation, GLM projection,
drag, chemistry, deposit, density assembly, FFT, gas gravity, and particle push.
Radiation predictor/corrector/ledger and optional chemistry subdivisions are
**nested breakdowns**, not extra phases to add again to the total.
{{< src "src/production/runner.jl" "function _time_phase" >}}

Fix diagnostic cadence and final outputs in comparisons. Portable spectrum
fallbacks may transfer full transformed grids to the host, while optimized
Metal spectrum binning remains on-device; the same table schema does not imply
the same overhead. FFT planning, allocation caches, data transfers, and initial
compilation must be distinguished from steady state.

## Memory budgeting {#sec-memory}

The nine Float32 MHD state arrays alone use 36 bytes/cell, excluding integrator
scratch, particles, gravity, chemistry, transforms, and diagnostics. For a
cubic grid the base four-channel radiation workspace approaches 32 bytes/cell
and four persistent half-complex photon fields add about 16 bytes/cell. Optional
three-component magnetic compensation adds 12 bytes/cell. These are component
estimates, **not a total resident-memory prediction**.

Use `MHD_MEMPROBE=1` and increasing small grids to measure the actual run.
Check both live and peak/cached allocations, OS memory pressure, and checkpoint
staging. Cubic scaling makes a factor-two grid refinement roughly eight times
as costly in cell storage. Keep substantial headroom; do not infer a safe
production grid from nominal unified memory or VRAM alone.

Avoid interpreting historical upstream M5 throughput, generic CUDA estimates,
or another package's bytes-per-cell model as a current PMFGLM measurement.
